messages:
alex: Quick question — do we want the fallback decision (canary -> full) to be made by the local frontend proxy or a centralized rollout arbiter?

maria: leaning central arbiter. easier to reason about global risk budgets. single place to enforce policy.

jonathan: but central adds latency and a single coord point. proxies can make fast heuristic decisions (e.g., error spike -> local immediate fallback).

hema: maybe hybrid? proxies handle immediate latency/error thresholds, arbiter handles gradual traffic shifts, canary quotas and coordinated rollbacks.

lucy: +1 hybrid. also need to think about signal visibility: proxies only see local tail latency, arbiter needs aggregated metrics to avoid premature rollbacks.

alex: tradeoffs I care about: correctness (no noisy rollback), speed (avoid long outage), operability (easy to debug), and reproducibility (replay decisions for postmortem).

maria: operationally, central arbiter gives reproducibility (single timeline of decisions). but we can log proxy heuristics to arbiter for audit.

jonathan: how about this split of responsibility: proxies implement deterministic short-circuit heuristics (circuit open on 5xx rate > 10% sustained for 10s), arbiter enforces percentage ramps and can force global rollbacks. proxies must accept arbiter overrides via a TTL'd policy.

hema: that seems reasonable. we need a clear API between arbiter and proxies. something like: GET /policy/:canary_id -> {allowed_pct, override_until, reason}. proxies poll every 5s and honor override_until.

lucy: polling is ok but adds a window where proxies act on stale info. could use long-poll or push via stream for urgent overrides. push for critical rollbacks only.

alex: here's a rough config we could standardize on:

```
canary_id: canary-2026-03-21-frontend
allowed_pct: 0.2
override_until: 2026-03-21T14:05:00Z
override_reason: "latency spike in eu-west-1"
heuristics: {
  local_error_threshold: 0.1,
  local_window_s: 10
}
```

jonathan: two more things: 1) we must avoid split-brain where proxies fallback but arbiter still ramps up traffic. add a token or revision number in the policy; proxies reject older revisions. 2) define metric staleness tolerance, e.g., proxies that lost telemetry should default to conservative fallback.

maria: good call. add policy_revision and min_telemetry_freshness_s. if telemetry older than X, proxies move to safe mode (allowed_pct=0).

hema: how about rollbacks initiated by arbiter also trigger a reconciliation job that slowly drains canary sessions from downstream (so in-flight KV caches are preserved)? we should avoid abrupt eviction.

lucy: that matches the product ask — graceful degradation. add handshake: arbiter sets transition_phase: {drain, immediate, monitor}. proxies act accordingly.

alex: imagining failure modes: - arbiter unreachable -> proxies should still follow last-known policy but enforce stricter local heuristics. - proxies partitioned -> arbiter sees partial metrics and must apply conservative global decisions.

jonathan: and telemetry: every decision (proxy or arbiter) must emit an event with decision_id. backend stores immutable decision timeline for audits and reruns.

maria: we'll need a small RFC for this. outline: responsibilities, policy schema, polling vs push, decision auditing, metric freshness rules, session drain handshake, invariants (no ramp > X without arbiter ok).

alex: can I get volunteers to draft the RFC? I'll draft sections on invariants and failure modes. maria can do policy schema. jonathan + hema work on proxy API and push vs poll. lucy documents product expectations (drain/monitor).

maria: happy to take schema. adding a note: keep schema simple so SDKs are tiny.

jonathan: ok will sketch proxy behavior and a minimal state machine.

hema: I'll cover telemetry flows and decision events.

lucy: I'll draft product acceptance criteria and a teardown plan.

sre-bot: reminder: create a post in #eng-releases when RFC is ready and add a follow-up meeting invite.

alex: thanks everyone. next check-in in ~48h. :thumbsup:
